name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q01 - Increasing order of penetrating power of radiations

questiontext.text:
Consider the following radioactive radiations emitted during the decay of radioactive substances:

(I) \(\alpha\)-particles
(II) \(\beta\)-particles
(III) \(\gamma\)-rays

Arrange these radiations in the correct increasing order of their penetrating power through matter:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Physical Nature of Radiations
Alpha (\(\alpha\)) particles are high-energy helium nuclei (\(\text{He}^{2+}\)) with relatively large mass and double positive charge. Beta (\(\beta\)) particles are fast-moving electrons carrying unit negative charge and negligible mass. Gamma (\(\gamma\)) rays are neutral, ultra-high-frequency electromagnetic photons carrying no charge and zero rest mass.

Step 2: Mechanism and Comparison of Penetrating Power
Due to their large mass and charge, \(\alpha\)-particles interact strongly with matter and produce intense ionization over short distances, causing them to possess the lowest penetrating power; they can be stopped by a thin sheet of paper or aluminum foil. In contrast, \(\beta\)-particles have much lower mass and charge, ionizing matter less strongly and possessing a penetrating power roughly 100 times greater than that of \(\alpha\)-particles. High-energy, uncharged \(\gamma\)-photons interact very weakly with atomic electrons, producing minimal ionization per unit length and exhibiting penetrating power roughly 1000 times that of \(\alpha\)-particles, requiring thick lead shielding to attenuate.

Step 3: Determination of the Correct Sequence
Arranging from lowest to highest penetrating power gives \(\alpha\)-particles, followed by \(\beta\)-particles, and finally \(\gamma\)-rays.

Final Answer:
The correct increasing order of penetrating power is \(\text{I} < \text{II} < \text{III}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q02 - Chronological sequence of historical atomic models

questiontext.text:
The following scientific milestones marked the historical development of atomic models and structural theory:

(I) Proposed nuclear model of the atom based on \(\alpha\)-particle scattering
(II) Formulation of Dalton's atomic theory of indivisible atoms
(III) Introduction of the quantum concept into atomic structure via quantized planetary orbits
(IV) Discovery of the neutron by bombarding beryllium with \(\alpha\)-particles
(V) Proposal of the uniform spherical positive charge "plum pudding" atomic model

Arrange these scientific developments in the correct chronological sequence from earliest to latest:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical Timeline of Each Milestone
- Dalton's atomic theory regarding the atom as the ultimate indivisible constituent of matter was proposed in 1808.
- J.J. Thomson proposed the uniform positive sphere model embedded with electrons ("plum pudding" model) in 1898.
- Ernest Rutherford presented the nuclear model of the atom following the gold foil \(\alpha\)-particle scattering experiments in 1911.
- Niels Bohr incorporated Planck's quantum concept to model discrete stationary orbits in the hydrogen atom in 1913.
- James Chadwick discovered the neutral fundamental particle, the neutron, in 1932.

Step 2: Sequential Ordering
Ordering the events strictly by their year of establishment gives:
1. Dalton's atomic theory (1808)
2. Thomson's plum pudding atomic model (1898)
3. Rutherford's nuclear model (1911)
4. Bohr's quantized atomic model (1913)
5. Chadwick's discovery of the neutron (1932)

Final Answer:
The correct chronological order is \(\text{II} \to \text{V} \to \text{I} \to \text{III} \to \text{IV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q03 - Increasing order of electromagnetic radiation frequencies

questiontext.text:
Consider the following regions of the electromagnetic spectrum:

(I) Ultraviolet radiation
(II) Microwaves
(III) X-rays
(IV) Radio waves
(V) Visible light

Arrange these radiations in the correct increasing order of their frequency (\(\nu\)):

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Relation
Electromagnetic radiation travels at a constant speed in vacuum (\(c = u \lambda\)). Therefore, frequency (\( u\)) is inversely proportional to wavelength (\(\lambda\)), and directly proportional to photon energy (\(E = h u\)).

Step 2: Characteristic Frequency Ranges
From the electromagnetic spectrum established in the NCERT curriculum:
- Radio waves: \(\approx 10^6 ext{ to }10^8 ext{ Hz}\)
- Microwaves: \(\approx 10^{10} ext{ Hz}\)
- Visible light: \(\approx 4 imes 10^{14} ext{ to }7.5 imes 10^{14} ext{ Hz}\)
- Ultraviolet radiation: \(\approx 10^{15} ext{ to }10^{16} ext{ Hz}\)
- X-rays: \(\approx 10^{18} ext{ to }10^{20} ext{ Hz}\)

Step 3: Ordering by Increasing Frequency
Comparing the frequency magnitudes gives:
\( ext{Radio waves} < ext{Microwaves} < ext{Visible light} < ext{Ultraviolet radiation} < ext{X-rays}\)

Final Answer:
The correct sequence of increasing frequency is \( ext{IV} < ext{II} < ext{V} < ext{I} < ext{III}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q04 - Increasing orbital energy order using n plus l rule

questiontext.text:
Consider the following atomic orbitals in a multi-electron atom:

(I) \(3d\)
(II) \(4s\)
(III) \(4p\)
(IV) \(5s\)

According to the Aufbau principle and the \((n+l)\) rule, arrange these orbitals in the correct order of increasing energy:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Application of the \((n+l)\) Rule
In multi-electron atoms, the energy of an orbital depends on the sum of principal quantum number (\(n\)) and azimuthal quantum number (\(l\)).
- An orbital with a lower value of \((n+l)\) possesses lower energy.
- When two or more orbitals have the same \((n+l)\) value, the orbital with the lower principal quantum number (\(n\)) has lower energy.

Step 2: Calculation of \((n+l)\) for Each Orbital
- For \(3d\) (Orbital I): \(n = 3, l = 2 \implies n+l = 3 + 2 = 5\)
- For \(4s\) (Orbital II): \(n = 4, l = 0 \implies n+l = 4 + 0 = 4\)
- For \(4p\) (Orbital III): \(n = 4, l = 1 \implies n+l = 4 + 1 = 5\)
- For \(5s\) (Orbital IV): \(n = 5, l = 0 \implies n+l = 5 + 0 = 5\)

Step 3: Comparison and Sequence Determination
- Orbital II (\(4s\)) has \(n+l = 4\), which is strictly smaller than \(5\); hence, it has the lowest energy.
- Orbitals I (\(3d\)), III (\(4p\)), and IV (\(5s\)) all share the identical sum \(n+l = 5\). Comparing their principal quantum numbers: \(n = 3\) for \(3d\), \(n = 4\) for \(4p\), and \(n = 5\) for \(5s\). Thus, their energies follow the order \(3d < 4p < 5s\).
- Combining these gives the full sequence: \(4s < 3d < 4p < 5s\).

Final Answer:
The correct increasing energy order is \(\text{II} < \text{I} < \text{III} < \text{IV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q05 - Decreasing order of wavelengths in Balmer series transitions

questiontext.text:
The following electron transitions occur in the emission spectrum of a hydrogen atom, all terminating at the lower energy level \(n_1 = 2\) (Balmer series):

(I) \(n = 3 \to n = 2\)
(II) \(n = 4 \to n = 2\)
(III) \(n = 5 \to n = 2\)
(IV) \(n = 6 \to n = 2\)

Arrange these transitions in the correct decreasing order of the wavelength (\(\lambda\)) of the emitted photon:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Relationship for Wavelength and Energy
The Rydberg formula for emission transitions in a hydrogen atom is given by:
\[\bar{\nu} = \frac{1}{\lambda} = R_{\text{H}} \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)\]
Alternatively, the emitted photon energy is \(\Delta E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\), which demonstrates that wavelength is inversely proportional to transition energy (\(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\Delta E}\)). A smaller transition energy difference produces a longer emitted wavelength.

Step 2: Comparison of Energy Differences (\(\Delta E\))
For each transition from initial level \(n_2\) to final level \(n_1 = 2\):
- \(n = 3 \to 2\): \(\Delta E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{5}{36} \approx 1.89\text{ eV}\)
- \(n = 4 \to 2\): \(\Delta E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{16}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{3}{16} \approx 2.55\text{ eV}\)
- \(n = 5 \to 2\): \(\Delta E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{25}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{21}{100} \approx 2.86\text{ eV}\)
- \(n = 6 \to 2\): \(\Delta E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{36}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{8}{36} \approx 3.02\text{ eV}\)

Step 3: Ordering Wavelengths in Decreasing Order
Since \(\Delta E_{3\to 2} < \Delta E_{4\to 2} < \Delta E_{5\to 2} < \Delta E_{6\to 2}\), the corresponding wavelengths follow the inverse order:
\[\lambda_{3\to 2} > \lambda_{4\to 2} > \lambda_{5\to 2} > \lambda_{6\to 2}\]
Here, \(n=3\to 2\) corresponds to the red \(\text{H}_\alpha\) line (\(\approx 656\text{ nm}\)), followed by blue-green \(\text{H}_\beta\) (\(\approx 486\text{ nm}\)), blue \(\text{H}_\gamma\) (\(\approx 434\text{ nm}\)), and violet \(\text{H}_\delta\) (\(\approx 410\text{ nm}\)).

Final Answer:
The correct decreasing order of wavelength is \(\text{I} > \text{II} > \text{III} > \text{IV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q06 - Operational steps in Millikan oil drop experiment

questiontext.text:
The following steps describe the operational procedure in R.A. Millikan's oil drop experiment used to determine the charge on an electron:

(I) Oil droplets acquire electrical charge by colliding with gaseous ions.
(II) An atomizer generates a fine spray of oil droplets into the upper chamber.
(III) A beam of X-rays ionizes the air molecules inside the observation chamber.
(IV) Droplets fall under gravity through a small aperture in the upper conducting plate.
(V) An adjustable voltage is applied across the plates to control and measure droplet motion.

Arrange these operational steps in the correct chronological sequence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Experimental Setup and Sequential Operation
In Millikan's apparatus, oil is initially vaporized into fine microscopic droplets inside the upper chamber using an atomizer. Next, these droplets descend under the influence of gravity, and a small fraction enters the viewing chamber below by passing through a tiny pinhole aperture located in the center of the upper circular plate.

Step 2: Charging and Observation Mechanism
Once droplets are between the two parallel plates, a collimated beam of X-rays is passed through the air to ionize gaseous molecules. The neutral falling droplets capture these gaseous ions (electrons or positive gaseous ions), thereby acquiring discrete negative or positive electrical charges. Finally, a high direct-current voltage is applied across the plates to establish an electric field, allowing the experimenter to arrest, retard, or accelerate the charged droplets to measure their terminal velocities and compute the net charge.

Step 3: Identification of Sequence
The logical sequence of events is:
1. Atomizer generates droplet spray (II)
2. Droplets descend through the aperture (IV)
3. X-ray beam ionizes the chamber air (III)
4. Oil droplets acquire charge via ion capture (I)
5. Electric potential applied to observe and measure droplet velocity (V)

Final Answer:
The correct operational sequence is \(\text{II} \to \text{IV} \to \text{III} \to \text{I} \to \text{V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q07 - Energy ordering of multi electron quantum states

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four sets of quantum numbers representing electrons in a multi-electron atom:

(I) \(n = 4, l = 0, m_l = 0, m_s = +\frac{1}{2}\)
(II) \(n = 3, l = 2, m_l = 1, m_s = +\frac{1}{2}\)
(III) \(n = 3, l = 1, m_l = 0, m_s = -\frac{1}{2}\)
(IV) \(n = 3, l = 2, m_l = -1, m_s = -\frac{1}{2}\)

In the absence of an external magnetic or electric field, arrange these electron states in the correct order of increasing energy:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying Orbitals from Quantum Numbers
- State I: \(n = 4, l = 0\) corresponds to an electron in the \(4s\) orbital.
- State II: \(n = 3, l = 2\) corresponds to an electron in a \(3d\) orbital.
- State III: \(n = 3, l = 1\) corresponds to an electron in a \(3p\) orbital.
- State IV: \(n = 3, l = 2\) corresponds to an electron in a \(3d\) orbital.

Step 2: Evaluating Energies via the \((n+l)\) Rule
In a multi-electron atom, subshell energy increases with the value of \((n+l)\). If \((n+l)\) values are identical, the subshell with the lower principal quantum number (\(n\)) has lower energy:
- For State III (\(3p\)): \(n+l = 3 + 1 = 4\)
- For State I (\(4s\)): \(n+l = 4 + 0 = 4\)
Between \(3p\) and \(4s\), both have \(n+l = 4\), but \(3p\) has lower \(n = 3\) compared to \(4s\) with \(n = 4\). Hence, \(E(3p) < E(4s)\), which means \(E_{\text{III}} < E_{\text{I}}\).

Step 3: Degeneracy of States within the Same Subshell
- For State II (\(3d\)): \(n+l = 3 + 2 = 5\)
- For State IV (\(3d\)): \(n+l = 3 + 2 = 5\)
Since \(n+l = 5\) is greater than \(4\), both \(3d\) states have strictly higher energy than \(3p\) and \(4s\). Furthermore, State II and State IV reside in the same \(3d\) subshell, differing only in magnetic quantum number (\(m_l\)) and spin quantum number (\(m_s\)). In the absence of an external magnetic or electric field, all orbitals within a given subshell are degenerate, meaning \(E_{\text{II}} = E_{\text{IV}}\).

Step 4: Assembling the Full Energy Relation
Combining the steps yields the exact relationship: \(E_{\text{III}} < E_{\text{I}} < E_{\text{II}} = E_{\text{IV}}\).

Final Answer:
The correct order of increasing energy is \(\text{III} < \text{I} < \text{II} = \text{IV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q08 - Increasing order of 2s orbital energy across atoms

questiontext.text:
Consider the energy of an electron occupying the \(2s\) atomic orbital in the following neutral atoms:

(I) Hydrogen (\(\text{H}, Z = 1\))
(II) Lithium (\(\text{Li}, Z = 3\))
(III) Sodium (\(\text{Na}, Z = 11\))
(IV) Potassium (\(\text{K}, Z = 19\))

Arrange these atoms in the correct order of increasing energy (from most negative to least negative / highest algebraic value) of their \(2s\) orbital:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Orbital Energy and Nuclear Charge
The energy of an electron in an atomic orbital is an attractive potential energy relative to an electron at infinite separation from the nucleus (assigned an energy of zero). As nuclear charge (\(Z\)) increases, the electrostatic attraction between the positively charged nucleus and an electron in a given principal energy level increases, pulling the electron closer and binding it more tightly.

Step 2: Variation with Atomic Number (\(Z\))
Because binding strength increases with increasing atomic number, the potential well deepens. Consequently, the energy of a given orbital (such as \(2s\)) becomes progressively more negative (lower in absolute value on the real number line) as the nuclear charge increases:
\[E_{2s} \propto -\frac{Z_{\text{eff}}^2}{n^2}\]
Hence, an atom with higher atomic number has a more negative (lower algebraic) orbital energy: \(E_{2s}(\text{K}) < E_{2s}(\text{Na}) < E_{2s}(\text{Li}) < E_{2s}(\text{H})\).

Step 3: Ordering from Lowest to Highest (Increasing Order)
- Potassium (\(Z = 19\)) has the largest nuclear charge, exerting the strongest attraction, so its \(2s\) orbital has the most negative energy (lowest energy).
- Sodium (\(Z = 11\)) has the next most negative energy.
- Lithium (\(Z = 3\)) follows.
- Hydrogen (\(Z = 1\)) has the smallest nuclear charge, exerting the weakest attraction, so its \(2s\) orbital has the least negative energy (highest algebraic energy).

Final Answer:
The correct order of increasing orbital energy is \(\text{IV} < \text{III} < \text{II} < \text{I}\).
